cards.front: Recall a key point about Issues & Debates in Psychology
cards.back: Nature vs nurture: nature argues behaviour is determined by inherited genes and biology; nurture argues behaviour is determined by experience and environment. Modern view: interactionism - both contribute. Epigenetics shows environmental factors can switch genes on/off, demonstrating that nature and nurture interact.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Issues & Debates in Psychology
cards.back: Free will vs determinism: free will argues people have conscious control over their choices; determinism argues behaviour is caused by factors beyond our control. Biological determinism (genes/neurochemistry), environmental determinism (conditioning), and psychic determinism (unconscious drives). Soft determinism (Bandura): some freedom within determined constraints.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Issues & Debates in Psychology
cards.back: Reductionism vs holism: reductionism explains behaviour by breaking it down into simpler components (biological reductionism: behaviour = brain chemistry). Holism argues the whole is greater than the sum of parts - behaviour must be understood as an integrated system. Reductionism is scientific but oversimplifies; holism is comprehensive but harder to test.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Issues & Debates in Psychology
cards.back: Ethnocentrism: judging other cultures by the standards of your own. Much research is WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic) and may not generalise. Example: Asch's conformity findings reflect 1950s America; collectivist cultures show higher conformity.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Issues & Debates in Psychology
cards.back: Gender bias: research that treats one gender as the norm (usually male = norm, female = deviation). Alpha bias: exaggerating differences between genders. Beta bias: minimising or ignoring differences. Examples: Kohlberg's moral development theory was based on male participants only; Milgram's study used only male participants but generalised to all people.

cards.front: What should you know about psychology exam tips?
cards.back: When discussing issues and debates, always: take a balanced position, use specific examples from research, and acknowledge that most debates are not either/or but exist on a continuum. The interactionist position is usually best supported by evidence.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: If behaviour is determined by biology and environment, then people cannot be held responsible for their actions. Correct: While determinism suggests behaviour has causes, this does not mean people lack all responsibility. Soft determinism (Bandura) argues we have conscious choice within constraints. cards.front: Assessment Objective Focus: Issues & Debates in Psychology
cards.back: AO1 — Knowledge: Demonstrate knowledge of Issues & Debates in Psychology including key definitions, research studies and psychological terminology.

cards.front: Key Studies and Theories in Issues & Debates in Psychology
cards.back: Issues & Debates in Psychology is a core topic in GCSE Psychology that requires understanding of key studies, theories and research methods. The AQA, OCR and Edexcel specifications all require you to know specific studies in detail, evaluate their methodology, and apply psychological concepts to real-life scenarios. When studying issues & debates in psychology, focus on: the aims, methods, results

cards.front: Evaluating Research in Issues & Debates in Psychology
cards.back: Evaluation is a crucial skill in GCSE Psychology. When evaluating studies related to issues & debates in psychology, use the GRAVE method: Generalisability (can the findings be applied to the wider population?), Reliability (are the results consistent if the study is repeated?), Applications (how can the findings be used in real life?), Validity (does the study measure what it claims to measure?),

cards.front: Applying Issues & Debates in Psychology to Real Life
cards.back: GCSE Psychology requires you to apply psychological understanding of issues & debates in psychology to everyday situations. Consider how the theories and studies you have learned about explain real behaviour: How does issues & debates in psychology affect people in schools, workplaces, families and communities?
